paras: The attempted lynching of Stephen Clutts was a threat by a mob against a man held at Marion, Williamson County, Illinois, in April 1888 on a charge of murdering his wife. A lynching party was organized on a Monday night, but the sheriff moved Clutts to the Johnson County jail before it acted. Two papers outside Illinois noted the case in short items, one calling the killing among the most brutal in the county's history.

News reached Marion on a Wednesday in early April 1888 that Clutts, who lived in the southern part of Williamson County, had killed his wife about two weeks before by beating her with the butt end of an ox whip-stock. The Indianapolis Journal's item called it "one of the most brutal murders ever committed in Williamson county." The grand jury then in session indicted him for murder, and the same report added that there was "talk of lynching."

After his arrest Clutts was taken to Marion and, according to a second report, held under guard there because Williamson County had no jail. On a Monday night, probably 9 April, a lynching party was organized to take him. The sheriff, "getting wind of the proposed action," slipped the prisoner away and carried him to the Johnson County jail. No attack on Clutts or on his guards is reported.
No report of Clutts's trial, verdict, or later fate appears in the coverage, and no arrests of members of the lynching party were reported.

The Indianapolis Journal carried both stages of the story as one-paragraph items in its Illinois "Brief Mention" column, first the murder and the talk of lynching on 7 April and then the foiled lynching party on 13 April. Neither item commented on the mob; the emphasis fell on the brutality of the murder and on the sheriff's removal of the prisoner. The Diamond Drill of Crystal Falls, Michigan, reprinted versions of both items in its regional news columns on 21 and 28 April; its first item, printed under an "Indiana" heading, left out the talk of lynching. None of the items named Clutts's race or gave the number or identity of the men in the lynching party.

The reports differ on where Clutts was first held: the 7 April item and its Michigan variant said he was "in jail in Marion," while the 13 April item said he was placed under guard because the county had no jail. The later account is more specific and is consistent with his removal to another county's jail, though neither came from a local paper.

bases: A lynching party was organized to take Clutts, held on a murder charge, and the sheriff removed him to another county's jail before any attack (A2); no one was killed.
A 'lynching party' formed against a man accused of murdering his wife, but the sheriff moved him away and no one was killed (A1, A2); the episode was a threatened lynching, not a completed one.
The organized lynching party is reported in one brief (A2), reprinted almost word for word in A4; A1's separate 'talk of lynching' supports the threat but not the details.

accounts.gist: News reached Marion on a Wednesday that Clutts had killed his wife about two weeks before; he was jailed at Marion and indicted, and there was 'talk of lynching'.

accounts.label: Report of the lynching party
accounts.gist: Clutts was held under guard at Marion because the county had no jail; a lynching party organized Monday night, and the sheriff took him to the Johnson County jail.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal ran the case as one-paragraph items in its Illinois 'Brief Mention' column, stressing the brutality of the murder and reporting the lynching plan without comment.
The Diamond Drill of Crystal Falls, Michigan, reprinted both briefs in its regional state-news columns a week or more later.
